“Today Michele and Stephany left us too soon. Thinking of their family, especially their children and parents,” Luque wrote on X.
Sensi-Contugi, 42, is a former businessman appointed as head of Ecuador’s National Intelligence Center in 2024. He was a close associate of right-wing President Daniel Noboa, whose country is mired in a security crisis.
US broadcaster NBCUniversal also said its journalist Jose Alberto Suarez – president and general manager of Telemundo 31, Telemundo 49, and Telemundo Fort Myers–Naples – was among those killed.
A spokesperson for the United States Department of State said five US citizens were among the dead.
“The US Embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” he said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”
![A rescue official works at the site of a tourist helicopter crash that caused multiple casualties, according to the police, in Samburu County, Kenya, August 19, 2026. Kenya Red Cross/Handout via REUTERS THIS IMAGE HAS BEEN SUPPLIED BY A THIRD PARTY. NO RESALES. NO ARCHIVES. MANDATORY CREDIT.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/reuters_6a85fbd0-1787165648.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C579&quality=80)
Recovery operations continue
The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported.
The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with travel company &Beyond. Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.
Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.
The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.
The Kenya Red Cross said that its emergency response teams were “participating in a multiagency response effort as rescue teams work to access the crash site”.
Three bodies were still trapped in the wreckage as of Wednesday evening, with recovery operations to continue on Thursday due to the ongoing flames at the crash site, Kenya’s Daily Nation reported.
In February, a Kenyan legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.
summary: A tourist helicopter crash in a remote part of Samburu County, Kenya, killed all seven people on board, including foreign tourists and officials. The aircraft went down while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area. Local authorities and aviation officials have launched an investigation into the incident.
key_points: Seven people died in the helicopter crash, including six passengers and the pilot.
The victims included an Ecuadorian intelligence official and his wife, as well as an American journalist.
The US State Department confirmed that five US citizens were among the dead.
The helicopter was a Eurocopter EC130 B4 operated by Lady Lori Helicopters on a charter flight for travel company &Beyond.

title: Ukrainian protesters reject Fedorov's call for wartime elections
author: Sasha Vakulina
content:
A month of nationwide demonstrations demanding Mykhailo Fedorov’s return as defence minister appears to be ending after protest organisers rejected and criticised his call for elections during wartime.
Mykhailo Fedorov’s call for wartime elections has been rejected by protesters who spent the past month campaigning for his return as defence minister.
The former minister’s video address on Tuesday evening marked an unexpected turn for a movement that had rallied behind him since Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed him in a wartime government reshuffle.
But leading organisers have opposed the idea of holding elections during the war and signalled an end to the daily demonstrations.
Dmytro Koziatynskyi, a Ukrainian war veteran and one of the protest organisers, said on Wednesday evening that he opposed holding elections while the war continued.
“I view elections during wartime negatively,” he wrote on X, adding that he could not “imagine how to technically enable thousands of soldiers currently on the front lines to vote and run for office”.
Four and a half years into Russia’s full-scale invasion, Koziatynskyi argued, Ukraine could not afford the divisions that an election campaign might create.
“In any case, street protests are definitely not the place for electoral discourse,” he said.
His statement appeared to draw a line under a month of daily demonstrations across Ukraine that began after Zelenskyy dismissed Fedorov from leading the defence ministry in mid-July.
Koziatynskyi stressed that the protests had been about the direction of Ukraine’s defence policy rather than Fedorov’s personal political future.
“These protests were specifically about dialogue and reforms, not about personalities,” he said.
He also offered his support to Yevhen Khmara, whom Zelenskyy formally nominated this week to replace Fedorov permanently.
“I want to wish Mr Khmara success in his new position and sincerely hope that he will continue the course on reforms and the fight against corruption in defence,” Koziatynskyi said.
Thanking those who had joined the demonstrations, he argued that the movement had nevertheless achieved tangible results, pointing to the dismissal of Oleksandr Syrskyi and the appointment of Mykhailo Drapatyi.
“I believe it was all worth it,” he said. “At the very least, we managed to secure the dismissal of Syrskyi and the appointment of Drapatyi, which hardly anyone could have expected just a month ago.”
'I did not go out for your political ambitions'
Fedorov’s address also prompted thousands of responses on social media, many questioning both the timing of his intervention and his motives for calling for elections only after his hopes of returning to the defence ministry had ended.
“Do you think this is a good time for an election campaign video?” one demonstrator wrote on Threads. Another commented telling Fedorov: “There is a feeling that you have taken too much upon yourself.”
Others questioned why Fedorov, after seven years in Zelenskyy’s team, had chosen to raise concerns about the political system only after the door closed on his possible return.
“So if you had been reinstated, you wouldn’t criticise the system and wouldn’t call for elections?” one user asked.
Some of those who said they had joined the demonstrations sought to distance the protest movement from any broader political ambitions Fedorov might harbour.
“I did not go out for your political ambitions, but for you to stay at the defence ministry,” one wrote.
“You shouldn’t have done it. This is populism,” another said.
Members of the Ukrainian military also questioned how elections could realistically be conducted while hundreds of thousands of troops are fighting off Russia's invasion.
One serviceman asked Fedorov whether soldiers should cast their ballots in “Kostyantynivka or Pokrovsk” - cities close to some of the heaviest fighting in eastern Ukraine.
The response from Zelenskyy’s administration was brief. Dmytro Lytvyn, a presidential adviser, told reporters in a WhatsApp group chat that Russia’s continuing attacks made the government’s position clear on any possible elections.
“The daily strikes by Russian drones and missiles provide a comprehensive answer.”
summary: Protesters who spent a month demanding Mykhailo Fedorov's return as defence minister have rejected his unexpected call for wartime elections. Organisers announced an end to the daily demonstrations, arguing that elections during the ongoing Russian invasion would cause dangerous divisions and make it impossible for frontline soldiers to vote. The protest movement clarified that their demonstrations focused on defence policy reforms rather than Fedorov's personal political ambitions, and they expressed support for his newly nominated successor, Yevhen Khmara.
key_points: Protest organisers rejected Mykhailo Fedorov's video address calling for wartime elections and signalled an end to a month of daily demonstrations.
Veteran and organiser Dmytro Koziatynskyi opposed elections due to the technical impossibility of frontline soldiers voting and the risk of domestic divisions.
Organisers stated the protests were about defence policy reforms and dialogue, not Fedorov's personal political future.
The movement expressed support for Yevhen Khmara, who was nominated to permanently replace Fedorov.
Fedorov faced criticism on social media from former supporters questioning the timing and motives of his election call.

title: Israel admits firing on car carrying Hind Rajab, symbol of Gaza’s suffering
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![Hind](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2025-09-03T155148Z_851274364_RC2FKGAAHC2Y_RTRMADP_3_FILMFESTIVAL-VENICE-THE-VOICE-OF-HIND-RAJAB-1787149476.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
More than two years after Hind Rajab was killed, becoming a symbol of the suffering of children in Gaza, Israel’s military, long accused of the atrocity, has announced a criminal investigation into the death of the five-year-old girl.
At first, Israel denied that its soldiers were even in the area where she was killed. After journalistic investigations, including by Al Jazeera, Israel’s army said it had raided “terror targets” in Gaza City that day. In January this year, Israeli officials said they were reviewing the case.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Hopes for justice rise as The Voice of Hind Rajab heads to Oscars
- list 2 of 3‘Substantial evidence’ of double-tap strike in killing of Hind Rajab
- list 3 of 3Gaza at the Venice Biennale: Where language falls short, threads take over
The military said in a statement on Wednesday that the criminal investigation into Rajab’s killing was decided on following a review of the findings “and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance”.
On January 29, 2024, at about 7:30pm, Rajab died of her injuries while she was trapped in a car surrounded by the bodies of her relatives, after her family was forcibly displaced hours earlier from Gaza City. They had attempted to follow Israeli orders to leave, but on their way, Israel’s army fired more than 300 bullets at the black Kia driven by Rajab’s uncle. Her 15-year-old cousin Layan was also in the car and spoke to Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) workers by phone before she was killed.
PRCS workers attempted to save Rajab, but were blocked from reaching her by Israeli forces. Palestinian paramedics dispatched an ambulance to rescue the child, the sole survivor, and stayed on the line until contact was lost.
The military said on Wednesday that troops had “fired at a vehicle that was approaching them”. It is the first time Israel has admitted shooting at the car.
But criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians rarely lead to convictions.
‘Complicit’
Decades of Israeli crimes against Palestinians have not delivered any serious form of justice, according to the president of the Hind Rajab Foundation, Dyab Abou JahJah, who does not believe this case will change that.
The foundation said it had no confidence in Israel’s decision to launch a criminal probe into Rajab’s killing.
“We do not trust the Israeli justice system, not out of an ideological position, but because of the track record,” Abou Jahjah told Al Jazeera. “And in this particular case, the Israeli justice system as a whole has always been complicit in Israeli crimes.”
Rajab’s grandmother, also named Hind Rajab, told The Associated Press news agency by phone that the Israeli investigation is not enough, and called for an international probe into the killing of her granddaughter and all of the thousands of children killed in Gaza during the war.
“An international investigation is required to uncover the truth and hold all those responsible accountable,” she said. “We call for justice, not only for Hind, but for all Gaza children.”
Rajab’s last words, her recorded pleas for help by phone, were widely shared on social media and led to international condemnation. A 2024 Al Jazeera investigation into the killing of Rajab and her family revealed that an Israeli tank was likely 13 to 23 metres (43 to 75ft) away and would have clearly seen the civilians inside the car. A docu-drama on the killing of Hind Rajab was nominated at the 2026 Oscars for best international feature film.
Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting in Gaza, said this sentiment is shared among Palestinians. “People here who are hearing about the investigation are sceptical that it will bring any justice to Hind and her family,” he said.
‘Intentional’ killings
Announcing its first criminal probes of troop conduct in Gaza, Israel’s military said the case of Rajab and her family members in early 2024 would be reviewed, as well as the killing of 15 Palestinian medics in March 2025. Both incidents gained international attention.
The announcement followed reviews of 150 incidents of troop conduct during Israel’s war on Gaza, it said, but added that the military would not launch criminal investigations into three other attacks that killed aid workers from the World Central Kitchen and Doctors Without Borders.
“The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” World Central Kitchen wrote on its website, disagreeing with the statement by the Israeli forces.
Israel “knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed,” said the non-profit, which provides people in need with fresh food. “The military investigation conflates different timelines and events, muddies the story and shifts the blame for the [Israeli army’s] illegal conduct.”
Australia on Thursday summoned Israel’s ambassador over the decision not to pursue criminal proceedings over the World Central Kitchen killings. Australian national Zomi Frankcom was among those killed.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the decision “falls far short of the accountability we expect”, adding that Australia was “outraged” by it.
In April 2024, seven international aid workers and a Palestinian driver were killed by three Israeli air strikes, despite driving in clearly marked cars and sharing their coordinates with the Israeli army.
An Al Jazeera investigation revealed the killings were intentional, directly opposing statements by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that described the targeting as “unintentional”.
summary: More than two years after five-year-old Hind Rajab and her relatives were killed in a car in Gaza City, the Israeli military has admitted firing at the vehicle and announced a criminal investigation. Initially denying its forces were in the area, the military stated the probe follows a review of findings and alleged failures in ambulance coordination. Family members, advocacy groups, and Palestinians remain skeptical about the investigation, with Rajab's grandmother calling for an international probe.
key_points: The Israeli military has admitted for the first time that its troops fired at the car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and her relatives in January 2024.
A criminal investigation into the killing has been announced following a review of findings and alleged coordination failures regarding a dispatched ambulance.
Hind Rajab became a global symbol of the suffering of children in Gaza after her recorded pleas for help were widely shared on social media.
Family members and the Hind Rajab Foundation expressed deep skepticism and a lack of trust in the Israeli justice system, calling instead for an international investigation.

title: Five Americans among seven killed in safari helicopter crash in Kenya
author: Associated Press; Guardian staff reporter
content:
Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya, according to local police and the state department.
Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.
The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.
Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.
In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”
The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.
“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.
The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.
Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.
Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.
The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.
Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.
In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”
Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.
Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.
In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.
summary: A safari helicopter crash in remote northern Kenya resulted in the deaths of all seven people on board, including five US citizens. The victims included a Telemundo executive and the director of Ecuador's national intelligence service, who was visiting with his wife. Kenyan aviation authorities and police have launched an investigation into the cause of the crash.
key_points: Seven people died when a charter helicopter crashed in Samburu county, Kenya.
The victims included five US citizens, among them a Telemundo executive.
Ecuador confirmed that the director of its national intelligence center and his wife were among the dead.
The aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4 operated by Lady Lori Helicopters.
Local authorities and the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority are investigating the crash.

title: ‘Nasty’ stories about Natalie Harp were leaked from White House, Laura Loomer says
author: Brendan Rascius
content:
The “nasty” stories about President Donald Trump’s executive assistant Natalie Harp are being leaked from inside the White House, Laura Loomer has claimed.
Loomer, a conservative activist and close Trump ally, alleged in a social media post that White House staffers are jealous of Harp, who has drawn intense media attention in recent months.
“Make no mistake, the nasty stories you’re seeing about Natalie Harp that are being posted are coming from inside the West Wing,” Loomer wrote on X on Wednesday. “A lot of the people who work for President Trump suffer from major professional jealousy and they are very bothered by loyalty.”
“How would anyone in the media know about Natalie’s work performance or have detailed accounts of her conversations with POTUS unless her colleagues are speaking badly about her?” Loomer continued. “Someone who works with her must want her job.”
Loomer, who has been known to propagate online conspiracy theories, went on to claim that Trump is surrounded by people who place their own ambitions over loyalty.
!['Nasty' stories about Natalie Harp, the president's executive assistant, are being leaked from inside the White House due to 'professional jealousy,' Laura Loomer has claimed](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/17/15/GettyImages-2287538819.jpeg)
“There are way too many leakers in the WH,” she wrote. “This is why vetting matters.”
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.
Harp, 35, reportedly helps manage Trump’s Truth Social account and handles a range of other administrative tasks for the president. In recent months, she has attracted intense media scrutiny, due in part to her near-constant presence at Trump’s side and what some perceive as an unusually fervent devotion to him.
In a recently published book, New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported that Harp was known to leave Trump adoring notes, including one that read: “You are all that matters to me.” The authors said they interviewed numerous Washington insiders for the book.
![Loomer, a right-wing political activist, wrote: ‘A lot of the people who work for President Trump suffer from major professional jealousy and they are very bothered by loyalty’](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/17/07/GettyImages-2256647474.jpeg)
Haberman has also referred to Harp, a former One America News Network presenter, as Trump’s “binkie” and “comfort blanket.” Her estranged brother, meanwhile, has described her relationship with the president as “very unhealthy.”
CNN also recently reported that, in 2023, Harp jumped into the trunk of an SUV when there was no space for her to ride in Trump’s motorcade to a court hearing in New York.
At the same time, Haberman has said Harp wields incredible power as a “conduit for information” to the president. “She is in almost every single — I mean, really I’m not kidding — almost every single meeting,” Haberman previously told MS NOW.
The White House, for its part, has vigorously defended Harp.
“No president has cultivated as much loyalty among their staffers and administration officials as President Trump; this is a testament to his commitment to our country and its people,” a White House spokesperson previously told The Independent. “Natalie Harp is a beloved White House Official, and the Fake News Media will never understand what it’s like to be as trusted and admired as her.”
![In recent months, Harp has attracted intense media scrutiny, due in part to her near-constant presence at Trump’s side and what some perceive as an unusually fervent devotion to him. Pictured: Trump and Harp walk after landing at the Ellipse near the White House on August 16](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/17/52/GettyImages-2290770431.jpeg)
Scrutiny of the president’s assistant intensified after it was reported that Harp was among a small group of aides chosen to accompany Trump aboard a military aircraft departing Turkey last month.
Senator Jon Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat, appeared to allude to the report at a rally over the weekend, claiming Trump “wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”
Several prominent conservatives objected to Ossoff’s jibe, including White House Communications Director Steven Cheung and CNN commentator Scott Jennings.
“Donald Trump has done more to elevate women in politics than any other President. Jon Ossoff is a despicable coward who thinks he can get ahead by smearing a cancer survivor and loyal public servant, Natalie Harp,” Jennings wrote on X. Harp survived bone cancer and has credited Trump’s right-to-try law with saving her life.
Not every Trump ally, however, was outraged by Ossoff’s comment.
“Am I fazed by this comment? No,” Fox News host Jesse Watters said Tuesday. “Has Trump said so much worse? So much more sleazy things against other people? Yes. Have I defended those things? Absolutely. So I’m not going to pretend I’m all hot and bothered about it, and the president doesn’t care.”
summary: Conservative activist Laura Loomer claimed that negative media stories about President Donald Trump’s executive assistant, Natalie Harp, are being leaked by jealous West Wing staffers. Harp has faced intense media scrutiny for her near-constant presence at Trump's side and her strong devotion to him. While critics and some reporters have questioned her role, the White House and conservative allies have vigorously defended her.
key_points: Laura Loomer alleged on social media that White House staffers are leaking negative stories about Natalie Harp out of professional jealousy.
Harp manages Trump's Truth Social account and handles administrative tasks while maintaining a near-constant presence at his side.
Recent books and media reports have highlighted Harp's close relationship with Trump and her detailed access to him.
The White House and prominent conservatives have defended Harp following scrutiny and recent remarks made by Senator Jon Ossoff.

title: Ecuador intelligence chief and five Americans killed in Kenya helicopter crash
author: Basillioh Rukanga; Thomas Mukhwana; Henry Moore
content:
![A rescue official works at the site of a tourist helicopter crash on a wooded hillside. The air is thick with smoke and there is wreckage on the ground.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/a600/live/64fb2200-9c07-11f1-b0bd-839fb1d8b591.jpg)
- Published
Ecuador's intelligence chief and his wife have been killed in a helicopter crash in Kenya.
Michele Sensi-Contugi and his wife Stephany Hollihan were among the seven people killed when the accident happened in Samburu county at approximately 09:13 (06:13 GMT) on Wednesday.
The other five victims were Americans, a US State Department spokesperson said.
The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) said the helicopter was on a scenic flight from a wildlife conservancy in Loisaba to Ewaso Nyiro, a river that flows along several national reserves.
![A map showing Mount Ololokwe and Kenya's capital, Nairobi](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/53b7/live/6b9bba60-9be5-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
Samburu county is a popular tourist destination with many private wildlife conservancies and is renowned for its stunning landscape.
Images from the scene show smoke at the wooded crash site on Mount Ololokwe, as members of the Kenya Red Cross approach the still-burning wreckage.
Ecuador has not given details about the death of Sensi-Contugi, 44, who was named director general of the Strategic Intelligence Center in 2024.
The president's office led tributes on behalf of the government to express sadness over the death of the intelligence chief.
Former President of Ecuador Guillermo Lasso mentioned he had died in the helicopter crash.
Lady Lori Helicopters, which operated the the Eurocopter EC130 B4 aircraft, said it was "deeply saddened" by the accident.
"Our deepest sympathies are with the guests, crew, their families and loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic accident," a statement read.
According to a memo seen by the BBC's US partner CBS News, external one of the Americans killed in the crash was NBCUniversal journalist JosÃ© Alberto SuÃ¡rez.
In the memo, NBCUniversal called SuÃ¡rez "a deeply respected leader and beloved friend and colleague.
"JosÃ© was an exceptional colleague and mentor to many," the memo read.
Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte was among the Americans killed in the crash, according to local and US media.
Commenting on his death on X, US Rep Carlos Antonio Gimenez wrote: "Our prayers are with their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time. May their memories be a blessing."
The four other American victims have not yet been identified.
Earlier reports had suggested seven people, six tourists and a pilot, were killed in the crash.
Helicopter crashes are not uncommon in Kenya.
In February, a helicopter crash in the Rift Valley county of Nandi killed six people, including a member of parliament.
In 2024, the military chief, Gen Francis Omondi Ogolla, died after an army helicopter that was carrying 11 people crashed in the west of the country, with only two survivors.
In June 2021 at least 10 soldiers were killed when their helicopter crashed while landing near the capital, Nairobi.
More about Kenya from the BBC:
![To the right of the banner a woman with sunglasses on her head and wearing a denim jacket and yellow T-shirt looks down at her mobile phone. A graphic for BBC News Africa in black and red is on the left of the image which has a pale golden brown background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/a743/live/681bd460-6ee0-11f1-8e1d-bbbb1017d210.png)
summary: Ecuador's intelligence chief, Michele Sensi-Contugi, and his wife were among seven people killed in a tourist helicopter crash in Samburu county, Kenya. The remaining five victims were US citizens, including NBCUniversal journalist José Alberto Suárez and Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte. The aircraft, operated by Lady Lori Helicopters, was on a scenic flight from a wildlife conservancy when it crashed on Mount Ololokwe.
key_points: Ecuadorian intelligence chief Michele Sensi-Contugi and his wife died in a Kenyan helicopter crash.
Five US citizens were among the seven total victims of the accident.
The victims included NBCUniversal journalist José Alberto Suárez and Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte.
The helicopter was operating a scenic flight in Samburu county when it crashed on Mount Ololokwe.

title: ‘No and no’: Fedorov’s wartime election call unsettles Kyiv
author: Daria Zakharova
content:
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov’s demand to hold wartime elections has sparked consternation in Kyiv, as the ramifications of a controversial government reshuffle rumble on.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s contentious ouster of Fedorov last month triggered nationwide protests — and has now resulted in the most serious internal challenge to his leadership since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.
Politicians from across the aisle chided Fedorov after the former minister’s call on Tuesday night to find a “legal, safe, and realistic mechanism” that would allow Ukraine to “resume a full-fledged democratic process, even amidst the ongoing war.”
summary: Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov's call for wartime elections has caused significant concern in Kyiv following his recent ouster by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Fedorov urged the creation of a mechanism to resume the democratic process despite the ongoing war. This demand and the preceding government reshuffle have sparked nationwide protests and represent a serious internal challenge to Zelenskyy's leadership.
key_points: Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for a mechanism to hold wartime elections in Ukraine.
Fedorov's demand unsettled Kyiv and drew criticism from politicians across the political spectrum.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent ouster of Fedorov previously triggered nationwide protests.
The ongoing political fallout represents the most serious internal challenge to Zelenskyy's leadership since the 2022 invasion.

title: Who is Natalie Harp? Trump's right-hand woman
author: Bernd Debusmann Jr
content:
![Natalie Harp walks off Air Force One wearing a sleeveless printed red dress. She is smiling and has a laptop in her hands.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/950/cpsprodpb/9db2/live/5fb103a0-9c02-11f1-b0bd-839fb1d8b591.jpg)
- Published
Few people in US President Donald Trump's orbit have appeared as frequently by his side as Natalie Harp in recent years.
One of Trump's longest-serving and most loyal aides, 35-year-old Harp is trusted with typing out his Truth Social posts, among other top responsibilities.
She was thrust again into the spotlight this week by Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff - a Democrat and frequent Trump foil - when he name-checked her during a speech that has since gone viral.
Ossoff attacked Trump's "travel with Natalie on their apparently defenceless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar", referring to the new Air Force One plane as well as to reports that Harp joined Trump - and a small group of people - when he secretly swapped planes leaving Turkey last month.
Here is what you need to know about the Trump assistant who has been called both a "gatekeeper" and a "comfort blanket".
Following an unorthodox path to the White House
A California native and member of a conservative Christian family, Harp followed an unorthodox path into an already unconventional White House.
She rose to fame by crediting Trump with saving her life.
In his first term, Trump got the Right to Try Act passed to give some patients greater access to experimental treatments, which Harp used for her bone cancer. She quickly gained prominence and popularity in Trump's Maga (Make America Great Again) wing of the Republican party talking about the experience, and soon after joined an advisory board for Trump's 2020 re-election campaign.
"When I failed the chemotherapies that were on the market, no one wanted me in their clinical trials," she said at the 2020 Republican National Convention. "They didn't give me the right to try experimental treatments, Mr President. You did, and without you, I'd have died waiting for them to be approved."
After the event, Trump said: "She lit up the television screen like very few people I have ever seen do it."
Following Trump's loss in that election, Harp found work hosting a show at the conservative One America News Network, or OAN.
There, she became known as a ferocious Trump defender and prominent election denier. She left the network in 2022 to join Trump's next presidential campaign.
Most accounts of Trump's views of Harp come via anonymous second-hand sources in books by reporters such as Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan or Michael Wolff, and very little is publicly known about her private life.
Now, Harp's official title at the White House is executive assistant to the president, which typically denotes a lower tier position that entails managing logistics, scheduling, communications flow and mundane - but vital - secretarial work.
By all accounts, though, Harp has given the role new meaning and her profile is significantly higher than that of her predecessors, such as Madeleine Westerhout in Trump's first administration.
How influential is Harp?
When a CNN reporter earlier this week asked Trump about Ossoff's comments, the White House reacted angrily later on its official X account, saying the reporter, Kristen Holmes, had taken a "cheap shot" at a staff member.
"Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question," another post directed to Holmes read. "They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive."
Harp's presence as a staffer is nearly constant in Trump's second term.
Reporters at the White House frequently see her standing just feet away from Trump in the Oval Office or boarding Air Force One for many of his domestic and international trips.
"She's always around," one source close to the White House told the BBC. "Literally, always."
Among White House insiders and members of the press, she is often referred to as the "human printer" because she is often spotted carrying a portable printer to provide Trump with hard copies of articles and social media posts, which he prefers.
In practice, this means that Harp has an outsized ability to control what information or updates Trump receives, according to another source familiar with White House operations.
Other anonymous sources have described her to US media outlets as a "gatekeeper" and "comfort blanket".
Harp also serves as something of a social media scribe for Trump, posting to his Truth Social account on his behalf.
In one image that has been widely shared in the aftermath of Ossoff's comments, Harp is shown typing a post - in the president's own writing style - as he dictates to her while watching a speech of Kamala Harris in 2024.
Amid the recent focus on Harp, the White House has described her as a "trusted and valued" member of the team, although Trump has rarely spoken about her on camera.
Ossoff was one of many Trump critics who noted Harp was reportedly on the plane that the president boarded to leave Turkey after the US supposedly received information about a threat from Iran.
Reporter Haberman, who has also reported extensively on Trump's presidencies, was asked during an appearance on the news network MSNOW why Trump took Harp with him on the secret plane: "Because she is sort of his binky, for lack of a better way of putting it, a comfort blanket."
Haberman and Swan reported for the New York Times in 2024 that Harp had supposedly written in a letter to Trump: "You are all that matters to me."
summary: Natalie Harp is one of Donald Trump's longest-serving and most loyal aides, serving as an executive assistant who manages his social media and provides him with printed news and online posts. She gained national prominence after crediting Trump's Right to Try Act with saving her life from bone cancer before later working for OAN and joining his campaign. Recently, her high-profile presence by Trump's side—including traveling with him on sensitive trips—has drawn increased public attention and criticism from political opponents.
key_points: Natalie Harp serves as an executive assistant to Donald Trump, often acting as his social media scribe and carrying a portable printer to provide him with hard copies of articles and posts.
She rose to fame during Trump's first term after crediting the Right to Try Act with giving her access to experimental treatments that saved her from bone cancer.
Before joining Trump's second-term White House staff, Harp worked as a host for the conservative One America News Network, where she was known as a fierce Trump defender and election denier.
She has been described by insiders and reporters as a 'gatekeeper,' 'comfort blanket,' and 'human printer' due to her constant proximity to Trump and her influence over the information he receives.

title: Natalie Harp stowed in trunk of SUV when Trump’s motorcade had no space: report
author: Owen Scott
content:
The estranged brother of Natalie Harp, Donald Trump’s doting aide, struggled to contain his laughter when told of the reported lengths his sister went to accompany Trump to a court hearing.
Preston Harp initially burst out laughing when CNN’s Erin Burnett asked for his reaction to the network’s report that his sister jumped into the trunk of an SUV when there wasn’t space for her to ride in Trump’s motorcade on the way to a court hearing in New York City in October 2023.
The network reports that a “screaming match” took place in the lobby of Trump Tower after there was no room for Natalie Harp in the motorcade. The aide reportedly insisted she had been asked by Trump to attend the hearing, but with no seat available, she climbed into the trunk of an SUV, according to sources and a photograph seen by CNN.
“That's really funny, I didn't know about that,” Preston Harp told CNN's Erin Burnett OutFront through laughter.
Burnett then asked him, “You're laughing, but I mean, is it funny or what? You know her, so that's why...”
![Preston Harp initially burst out laughing when CNN’s Erin Burnett asked for his reaction to the network’s report](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/14/22/preston-harp.png)
“No, it’s not, I'm sorry, it’s actually sad,” Preston Harp added. “That’s obsession. That’s like an unhealthy obsession with someone if you’re going to jump into the trunk of their car.”
Natalie Harp’s estranged sibling, a Trump critic, also detailed more about his upbringing with his sister, claiming that his mom believed in American exceptionalism.
“Trump is like everything that my mom taught us to respect,” he said. “I think that's where her infatuation with Trump comes from, honestly.”
The reported trunk incident is another example of Natalie Harp’s devotion to the president, which has “unnerved” some of her White House colleagues, according to The New York Times.
She has come under the spotlight this week, with multiple reports detailing how she became one of his most trusted supporters. The executive assistant is often seen by the president’s side, having cultivated a close working relationship since she first came to Trump’s attention in 2019.
She joined Trump’s staff in 2022, having claimed he “saved her life” after she was diagnosed with stage II bone cancer. She hit the headlines earlier this month when it emerged she was one of a small number of aides who were transferred to a military plane in Turkey to avoid a suspected assassination threat by Iran.
One unnamed White House advisor told CNN that Trump “likes the attention and the fact that she is 100 percent committed and loyal.”
“She doesn’t second-guess, doesn’t question,” the advisor said of Natalie Harp, who has also reportedly earned the nickname of “human printer” for handing the president hard copies of social media posts and newspaper articles.
Democratic senator Jon Ossoff drew further attention to Natalie Harp this week after suggesting at a rally Trump would rather fly with “Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace” than do his job.
The Trump administration has vociferously defended her, with the official Rapid Response 47 account on X tearing into a CNN correspondent who asked the president about the aide.
She was described as “one of the most loyal and hardest working aides on President Trump’s team” in a statement by White House spokesman Davis Ingle this week.
And Ossoff, meanwhile, was branded a “radical, extremist Dumocrat” by White House communications director Steven Cheung in a social media response to his speech.
summary: Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp reportedly climbed into the trunk of an SUV during an October 2023 motorcade in New York City after discovering there was no room for her to ride inside. Her estranged brother, Preston Harp, reacted to the report by calling it an unhealthy obsession, while administration officials have strongly defended her loyalty and hard work. Harp is known for her close devotion to Trump, having joined his staff in 2022 after previously crediting him with saving her life.
key_points: Natalie Harp reportedly climbed into the trunk of an SUV to accompany Donald Trump to an October 2023 court hearing when no seats were available in the motorcade.
Her estranged brother, Preston Harp, initially laughed at the report before describing her behavior as an unhealthy obsession.
White House officials and a spokesperson strongly defended Harp, describing her as one of the president's most loyal and hardworking aides.
Harp joined Trump's staff in 2022 after previously stating that he saved her life following her bone cancer diagnosis.

title: Israel admits its soldiers fired at car in which Hind Rajab was killed
author: Jason Burke
content:
The Israeli military admitted on Wednesday its troops had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, saying it had ordered a criminal investigation into the killing.
The killing of Hind and her family was one of the most high profile of a series of incidents involving civilian casualties during the first months of the Gaza conflict which prompted international outrage.
Hind died after a desperate three-hour phone call to the Palestinian Red Crescent on 29 January 2024 in which she pleaded for rescue. The family’s Kia Picanto car had been hit as the family sought to flee a new Israeli offensive into Gaza City. All the other passengers were also killed.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) repeatedly denied its troops had been present in the area near the incident, but investigations by media and others found evidence that strongly suggested nearby Israeli tanks were responsible.
![A boy peering in to a badly damaged car](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/725e85c027588ab32e48df1d9fdccb22c6a0342d/134_0_4583_3667/master/4583.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Palestinian paramedics dispatched an ambulance to rescue Hind and stayed on the line until contact was lost, but the ambulance too came under fire, killing two medics. The bodies of the casualties were only retrieved 12 days later when Israeli troops withdrew. The IDF also admitted Wednesday that troops had fired on the ambulance.
“Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by military police criminal investigation division,” the military said on Wednesday.
Criminal misconduct investigations into Israeli troops over the killing of Palestinians rarely lead to convictions.
The IDF published reviews on Wednesday into four other high-profile incidents in Gaza, saying it was launching a criminal investigation into the killing in near the southern city of Rafah of 15 Palestinian medics and humanitarian personnel in March 2025.
Troops lying in ambush for Hamas militants initially shot at an ambulance that was trying to retrieve casualties from an Israeli offensive, then fired on a series of emergency vehicles which approached their positions, according to phone footage and the sole survivor of the shootings.
The soldiers then bulldozed over the bodies and vehicles, burying them in a mass grave. UN and rescue workers were only able to reach the site a week later.
“They were killed in their uniforms. Driving their clearly marked vehicles. Wearing their gloves. On their way to save lives. This should never have happened,” said Jonathan Whittall, a UN official who helped recover the bodies.
The Israeli military initially said it had opened fire because the vehicles were “advancing suspiciously” without headlights or emergency signals. But it backtracked from that account after footage emerged showing the Red Crescent and civil defence teams driving slowly with their emergency vehicle lights flashing and logos visible.
![Two Red Crescent paramedics standing by a mound of bulldozed sand with the ruins of vehicle protruding](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ed89174c94a3296839d12e1eebb001ff6fbc0cb5/80_0_1501_1200/master/1501.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Munther Abed, a Palestinian paramedic who was present at the incident in which 15 of his colleagues were killed, said he hoped “those who killed my colleagues, who were like family to me, face justice, real justice”. “I want to say to the whole world, ambulances 101 is not a target and they must be protected,” he said referring to the speed dial number for the Red Crescent service in Gaza.
The IDF said it had decided not to open a criminal investigation into the April 2024 airstrikes that hit a convoy of World Central Kitchen vehicles, killing seven humanitarian workers from the US-based aid group, which has distributed food in Gaza throughout the war.
The aid group said at the time it had coordinated with the military over the movement of its cars. The vehicles, which had the group’s logo on their roofs visible from the air, were left incinerated and mangled, indicating a series of targeted strikes.
![A shot from above showing a vehicle bearing the World Central Kitchen logo on its roof punctured by large, charred hole](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/8984c1050795fe2ca42e3514e97055aaeb892e0f/173_0_2400_1920/master/2400.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The IDF said on Wednesday it had mistaken several individuals in the vehicles for armed Hamas military operatives, and that the convoy deviated from the previously coordinated route. But it concluded that “the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct”. Two officers were removed from their positions at the time and three others reprimanded.
World Central Kitchen said it strongly disagreed with Israeli officials’ account of the airstrikes and their decision not to pursue a criminal investigation. “There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive,” it said in a statement.
“At the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody. It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”
The military also decided not to take criminal action over the killing of four humanitarian workers from Doctors Without Borders in two separate instances in November 2023 and February 2024. Israel later effectively barred the medical charity from operating in Gaza.
Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din, an Israeli rights organisation, said that over the last decade only a tiny proportion of investigations had led to indictments while growing political pressure “further deters Israeli law-enforcement authorities from holding those responsible accountable, even when clear evidence does exist”.
A UN report published in February described “a pervasive climate of impunity” by Israel in occupied Palestine “in relation to gross violations of international human rights law and serious violations of international humanitarian law … some constituting war crimes and possibly other international crimes”.
Israeli forces say they never deliberately target civilians in Gaza and accuse Hamas of using civilians to shield its militants.
The IDF said that as part of the its obligations under international law and Israeli domestic law, it examined “exceptional incidents that occurred during combat”. “For more than a thousand days, the IDF has been conducting intensive combat across numerous fronts, carrying out a wide range of military missions in an exceptionally complex operational reality,” it said in a statement.
The war began in October 2023 when Hamas launched a surprise attack into southern Israel, killing 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and abducting 250. Israel’s ensuing offensives in Gaza have killed more than 73,000, mostly women and children, including more than 1,200 since a fragile ceasefire took effect in October.
On Wednesday, Israeli airstrikes killed seven Palestinians. Israeli military officials told local media one strike that killed six had targeted a meeting of Hamas commanders in Gaza City.
summary: The Israeli military admitted that its troops fired on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza in 2024, as well as on the ambulance dispatched to rescue her, and announced a criminal investigation. The IDF also released reviews of other high-profile incidents, initiating a criminal investigation into the killing of 15 medics near Rafah while declining criminal actions for strikes on World Central Kitchen workers and Doctors Without Borders staff. Rights organizations and UN reports have highlighted a broader climate of impunity regarding military accountability in the ongoing conflict.
key_points: The IDF admitted troops fired on Hind Rajab's family car and a subsequent rescue ambulance, prompting a criminal investigation.
A separate criminal investigation was opened into the killing of 15 Palestinian medics and humanitarian personnel near Rafah.
The military declined to open criminal investigations into airstrikes that killed World Central Kitchen humanitarian workers and Doctors Without Borders staff.
Human rights groups and UN reports have criticized a pervasive climate of impunity and low rates of indictments regarding Israeli military conduct in the Palestinian territories.

title: Trump pauses 50pc tariffs on Canada after ‘deal’
author: US Staff
content:
![Donald Trump, pictured with Mark Carney last October, has called Canada's prime minister 'nasty'](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/en-us/news/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000497661915_17871086961640_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq_9wf_3J7sd4A4L08_4VHg9f11FLKtqwYaxK652uKeQE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Donald Trump, pictured with Mark Carney last October, has called Canada's prime minister 'nasty'](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/en-us/news/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000497661915_17871086961640_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq_9wf_3J7sd4A4L08_4VHg9f11FLKtqwYaxK652uKeQE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Donald Trump has paused the US plan to impose 50 per cent tariffs on Canada after claiming the two countries had struck a deal.
The US president said on Tuesday night that he would freeze the tariffs, which had been due to come into force on Wednesday, for three days, because an agreement had been reached on the Keystone XL Pipeline.
On his Truth Social network, Mr Trump wrote: “I have paused the 50 per cent tariffs against Canada, that were scheduled to kick in tomorrow morning for a three-day period, based on the fact that Canada and the USA, subject to the finalisation of documents, have a DEAL!
“The great Keystone XL Pipeline, long ago killed by Sleepy Joe Biden, may be awoken from the grave!”
On Wednesday, Mr Trump told reporters that he had “come to a deal with Canada.
“Canada was charging us tremendous tariffs. We no longer have any tariffs ... it’s all subject to the finalisation of documents,” he said.
The planned 1,200-mile pipeline extension would carry almost a million barrels of crude oil per day across the border from Alberta to Nebraska.
It was blocked in 2021 by the Biden administration under pressure from indigenous communities and environmental groups but Mr Trump has been keen to revive the plan.
There was no immediate comment or confirmation from the Canadian government.
Jamieson Greer, the US trade envoy to Canada, said the deal would include “comprehensive market access” for all American goods, economic security commitments and alignment on digital trade.
After more than a week of meetings and technical negotiations, Canada had been braced for the punishing tariffs to take effect at 12.01am on Wednesday.
It was understood that Canada had been prepared to offer concessions to prevent the tariffs taking effect, and to have levies on Canadian goods lifted.
Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, had described the negotiations as “very delicate and intense”.
On Tuesday afternoon, the White House was presented with a proposal to end the tariffs, a US official told The New York Times, and Mr Trump and Mr Carney spoke on the phone in a last-ditch effort.
Mr Trump has frequently targeted Mr Carney in public since the former governor of the Bank of England took office last spring, calling him “nasty”. The US president has previously threatened to make Canada the US’s “51st state”.
The tariffs of 50 per cent on goods including hockey sticks were announced last month by the White House.
They would have accounted for about $20bn (£15bn) of annual trade, and 2 per cent of the trade between the two countries. Canada is the US’s second-biggest trading partner.
They would have applied in addition to the 50 per cent tariffs that Mr Trump had already imposed on Canadian industries, such as steel, lumber and carmakers.
The dispute relates to the collapse in the free trade agreement between the two countries and Mexico, which must now be renewed annually.
Mr Trump also vowed last month to impose tariffs because smoke from Canadian wildfires was crossing the border into the Midwest and north-east US.
It was reported that one of the main sticking points in the negotiations had been American tariffs on Canadian vehicles.
The sides discussed cutting US Section 232 tariffs on Canadian vehicles to 15 per cent from 25 per cent, with further reductions based on the amount of American content in each vehicle, Reuters reported.
The deal, if agreed, looks set to end a bitter row between the US and Canada over the Keystone XL Pipeline.
On Tuesday night, Mr Trump shared an illustration on his Truth Social page that depicted him resurrecting the pipeline:
summary: Donald Trump has paused a planned 50 per cent tariff on Canada for three days after announcing that a preliminary deal has been reached. The agreement centers on the potential revival of the Keystone XL Pipeline and includes commitments on market access, economic security, and digital trade. Final documentation of the deal is still pending, and the Canadian government has not yet provided immediate comment.
key_points: Donald Trump paused 50 per cent tariffs on Canada for three days following a reported agreement.
The deal includes an agreement regarding the Keystone XL Pipeline, which was previously blocked in 2021 by the Biden administration.
US trade envoy Jamieson Greer stated the deal involves comprehensive market access for American goods and alignment on digital trade.
Negotiations followed intense discussions between Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to avert punishing trade levies.

title: US-led drills to end six days early, South Korea says, amid Trump push for Kim Jong-un talks
author: Raphael Rashid
content:
South Korea’s military has confirmed that joint military drills with the US will be cut short, days after Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back the exercises.
In a statement on Wednesday, South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff said at the request of the US side, the Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise – which began on Monday would end on Friday, six days earlier than originally planned.
Separately, joint field training exercises, live outdoor drills held alongside the simulated command exercise, would also be “partially reduced”, though the two militaries were still working out the details, the statement said.
A Pentagon official later confirmed the US military was “substantially” reducing joint exercises with South Korea.
Trump said on Sunday he was “not happy” with US participation in the exercise, citing his “very good relationship” with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, and describing the drills as costly and “hostile” toward Pyongyang.
South Korea’s foreign minister, Cho Hyun, told a parliamentary hearing on Wednesday that Seoul had been caught off guard by Trump’s directive.
“Our government officials, of course, and the US government officials hadn’t known about it in advance”, Cho said, when asked whether Seoul had been informed.
![US army soldiers conduct a training exercise on a river in Yeoncheon, South Korea, near the border with North Korea, on Tuesday.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ed0f98e8e5dc70502242d9bd495eeca42574d678/0_0_8640_5760/master/8640.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Ahead of Wednesday’s announcement, South Korean broadcasters KBS and MBC and the newspaper Kyunghyang reported, citing unnamed military sources, that the exercise’s second stage, a simulated counterattack against North Korea that Pyongyang has always denounced most sharply, would be scrapped entirely and bring the exercise to an early end.
Days before the exercise began, Lt Gen Scott Winter, deputy commander of the United Nations Command, the multinational body that oversees the armistice and contributes personnel to the exercise, described this year’s UFS exercise as “bigger and better than ever”.
The US military presence in South Korea dates back to the Korean war, which ended in an armistice rather than a formal peace treaty in 1953, meaning the two Koreas remain technically at war.
US troops have been stationed in South Korea ever since, and the country now hosts Camp Humphreys, the largest American military base outside the US. The two militaries train and operate together closely, including through large-scale annual exercises such as this week’s.
Previous cuts and cancellations to joint exercises, including in 1992, 1994 and after Trump’s first summit with Kim in 2018, were all decided before the drills began, rather than after they were already under way.
Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Trump was pushing aides to arrange a meeting with Kim as early as the northern hemisphere autumn, citing unnamed US officials.
The paper said Trump had privately discussed an in-person meeting to take place during his next trip to Asia, which could be in November when he is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, China.
![Trump meets with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un at the border of North and South Korea in 2019.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/8d4cd05294a5e8be4b529e5a6aca3d0ae2032f10/0_0_4252_2835/master/4252.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Earlier, a social media post from Trump showing an image of Kim surrounded by military officials, speaking into a telephone, captioned “Hey Donald, we cool … right?”.
Trump also told reporters Kim had “responded” to his overtures for talks, though he declined to give details.
Trump met Kim three times during his first term, including a brief crossing into North Korean territory at the demilitarised zone in 2019. Speculation about a renewed summit has grown since Trump shared an old photograph of the pair together on Truth Social last weekend.
Cheong Seong-chang, the vice-president of the Seoul-based Sejong Institute thinktank, said Trump could go further if talks with Kim resumed, potentially suspending the joint exercises altogether or reducing US troop numbers without consulting Seoul.
South Korea’s presidential office said this week it would continue to coordinate with Washington on the exercises as president Lee Jae Myung separately renewed calls for greater military independence.
summary: South Korea's military has confirmed that joint UFS drills with the United States will end six days early at the request of the US. The decision follows Donald Trump's order to scale back the exercises due to his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and his push for potential talks. South Korean officials stated they were caught off guard by Trump's directive, which also involves partially reducing joint field training.
key_points: Joint US-South Korean military drills are ending six days early at the request of the US.
Donald Trump ordered the reduction citing his relationship with Kim Jong-un and describing the exercises as costly and hostile.
South Korea's foreign minister stated that government officials in Seoul were not informed in advance.
Reports indicate Trump is also pushing aides to arrange a potential in-person meeting with Kim Jong-un as early as autumn.

title: Erin Patterson: 'Catastrophic' hotel blunder caused unfair trial, mushroom murderer's lawyers tell court
author: Live Reporting Edited by Joel Guinto; With Katy Watson; Simon Atkinson
content:
The first day of Erin Patterson's appeal hearing has ended. Here's what you need to know:
- Patterson was sentenced to life in prison last year for murdering several relatives with deadly mushrooms concealed in a beef Wellington lunch
- Her lawyers are appealing her sentence, arguing that there was a "substantial miscarriage of justice" at her trial
- The jury accidentally stayed at the same hotel as prosecutors and a key police witness - which Patterson's lawyers today said was "catastrophic" to the integrity of the trial. But prosecutors pushed back against this claim, saying there was no evidence of interaction between the jurors and those guests
- Here's a summary of the key arguments made today, and how they went down with the appeals court judges
- Patterson attended the hearing via video link from a maximum security prison
- Also in court was Ian Wilkinson, the sole survivor of the fateful mushroom lunch
- The prosecution is mounting its own appeal, arguing that Patterson should not be eligible for parole. Her current sentence allows for parole after 33 years
summary: Erin Patterson's lawyers are appealing her life sentence for murder, arguing that a "substantial miscarriage of justice" occurred because the jury accidentally stayed at the same hotel as prosecutors and a key police witness. Prosecutors pushed back against the claim, stating there is no evidence of interaction. Meanwhile, the prosecution is mounting its own appeal to deny Patterson parole eligibility.
key_points: Erin Patterson is appealing her life sentence for murdering relatives with poisoned mushrooms.
The defense argued that the jury staying at the same hotel as prosecutors and a key police witness was a "catastrophic" blunder.
Prosecutors stated there is no evidence of interaction between the jurors and the other guests.
The prosecution is separately appealing to make Patterson ineligible for parole.

title: Israel confirms it opened fire on vehicle carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza
author: Yolande Knell
content:
![Hind Rajab smiles at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/755/cpsprodpb/a318/live/339ec150-9bc9-11f1-98c6-93bfcdb08681.jpg)
- Published
The Israeli military has confirmed for the first time that it opened fire on a vehicle carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six members of her family in Gaza City during the war in Gaza.
The Palestinian child initially survived the attack in January 2024 that killed several family members, but her body was recovered days later along with her relatives.
After the attack, Hind managed to answer a telephone call from the Palestinian Red Crescent Society, which lasted hours. An ambulance it sent to reach her â in a move coordinated with the Israeli army - was then shelled, killing two paramedics.
In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that following a review it would be opening a criminal investigation.
"Due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division", it said.
The IDF initially stated that none of its troops were in the area at the time of Hind's killing. However, that suggestion was soon questioned.
The IDF later said it had "conducted raids on terror targets" with forces operating in neighbourhoods in Gaza City, including Tel al-Hawa, where Hind was located.
Hind's killing was internationally condemned after a desperate recording of her speaking to paramedics was broadcast around the world.
She and her family were trying to flee the Israeli invasion of their neighbourhood in Gaza City, when their vehicle came under Israeli fire.
Hind's pleas for someone to rescue her ended when the phone line was cut amid the sound of more gunfire.
The story was made into an Oscar-nominated film called The Voice of Hind Rajab.
The UN cited her case in a commission of inquiry, accusing Israel of war crimes, which it denies.
Aside from the criminal investigation into Hind and her family, the IDF also said it would investigate the killing of 15 Palestinians, including medics and a UN worker near Rafah in southern Gaza last year.
In three other cases, involving the killing of seven World Central Kitchen employees in Deir al-Balah two years ago, and four employees of MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF), who were killed in two incidents, the IDF said it had not found grounds for criminal investigations.
The IDF is under pressure to show it investigates itself to try to stave off international legal action, most notably from the International Criminal Court.
It aims to counter accusations that it has committed war crimes and that there is impunity for its forces.
Correction: The initial version of this story and breaking news notification said Hind Rajab was aged six. The copy was updated after it was later confirmed she was aged five
summary: The Israeli military has confirmed for the first time that it opened fire on a vehicle carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and six family members in Gaza City in January 2024. Although Hind initially survived the shooting, she and an ambulance sent to rescue her by the Palestinian Red Crescent Society were subsequently killed. Following a review, the Israel Defense Forces announced it is opening a criminal investigation into the incident.
key_points: The IDF confirmed it fired on the vehicle carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab and her family.
An ambulance sent to rescue Hind was shelled, resulting in the deaths of two paramedics.
The IDF announced a criminal investigation will be conducted by the Military Police Criminal Investigation Division.
The UN previously cited Hind's case in a commission of inquiry, accusing Israel of war crimes.
